19812-the-south-and-the-national-governm:
William Howard Taft wrote The South and the National Government as a sitting president. It argues for restoring normal political conditions in the South. Taft is described as a man of sound judgment and lofty purpose. The writer professes himself sanguine of success under Taft's leadership. Support from influential people of all sections is urged. The essay dates from Taft's first year, 1909.

After Reconstruction, the South voted as one party's bloc. Taft hoped to loosen that pattern with appointments and goodwill. His essay addresses Southern readers directly and respectfully. It is a primary document of his Southern strategy. Historians of the era still weigh its hopes against results. The tone is conciliatory to a degree later readers may question.
19861-the-lady-paramount:
Henry Harland wrote The Lady Paramount in 1902, a novel of manners. Precedence, who ranks above whom, opens its social game. A fond old man admires how the lady waives her rightful precedence. She yields it in favor of her senior, handsomely. He transfers his attention to the Baroness instead. Such gestures carry whole plots in Harland's world.

Harland edited The Yellow Book and wrote of Italy and society. His ladies paramount rule rooms by charm and rank. The novel plays courtesy as both art and weapon. Readers who enjoy Jamesian nuance will find kinship here. Harland's touch is lighter, his wit quicker. The book preserves a polished Edwardian manner now extinct.
19916-civilization-tales-of-the-orient:
Ellen N. La Motte published Civilization: Tales of the Orient in 1919. One tale recalls Shanghai a generation earlier. The city then was not as respectable as it later became. A young man fresh from Home meets its crude pleasures and companions. The shock of that meeting drives the story. La Motte, a nurse and writer, knew Asia from wartime service.

La Motte's Orient is no travel-poster fantasy. Her tales show empire's boredom, vice, and self-deception. She writes white expatriate life with a scalpel. The Shanghai of treaty-port days gets no mercy. Critics rank her among the sharpest short-story stylists of her time. These tales justify that rank.
20224-the-invisible-government:
Dan Smoot published The Invisible Government in 1962, a warning about hidden power in America. Smoot claims a small, linked group steers the nation from behind scenes. His book tells who they are and how they work, he says. If enough Americans knew, he argues, the Republic would be saved.

He urges readers to order extra copies and spread the word widely. Quantity prices sit inside the back cover for that very purpose. The book names councils and networks as the core of its case. Readers get a key text of 1960s American anti-elite politics, in full voice.
20461-german-culture-past-and-present:
Ernest Belfort Bax wrote German Culture: Past and Present to trace the growth of German thought and society. Bax was a socialist historian with a deep interest in the Reformation age. The book moves from medieval Germany toward modern times.

Bax notes that the close of the fifteenth century left the whole structure of medieval Europe looking intact. Statesmen and writers like Philip de Commines had little suspicion that the world around them was about to break. From that false calm, the book follows the upheavals that remade German life, in church, state, and ideas.
20900-english-past-and-present:
More fixes were needed in English Past and Present than in The Study of Words, its author owns. Sweeping claims that a word was born or died in one year invite error. Richard Chenevix Trench flags that risk in his own preface with candour.

Trench, an archbishop and word lover, traces how English grew and changed. Old senses, lost words, and new coinages fill his lively survey. His books helped spark the great Oxford English Dictionary project. Readers who love words will find him a warm guide, keen to show that a tongue's past lives in its present speech.
20910-south-american-fights-and-fighters:
The Spanish Main means mainland, not sea, says Cyrus Townsend Brady in South American Fights and Fighters. Shakespeare's use in Othello misleads most readers on the phrase, he argues. Brady opens his 1910 tales by clearing that point with zest.

Sea fights, conquistadors, and bold deeds across South America fill the tales. Brady loved martial history and tells it at a gallop. Pirates, patriots, and fleets clash from the Caribbean to the Pacific coasts. Readers who like old-school adventure history will find Brady in his element, learned, breathless, and keen to honour daring on every page.
21025-the-village-wife-s-lament:
A bow as red as a blood-soaked sword hangs in The Village Wife's Lament, a war poem. What should God grant, it asks, to a brood thus Cain-branded by slaughter? The rainbow of peace twists here into a sign of wrath rekindled.

Mona Caird wrote this lament in a wife's voice amid the Great War's grief. Village homes emptied of men give the poem its bitter ground. Brief and fierce, it stands among the sharpest home-front protests of its war. The poem speaks from the home front.
21291-pushing-to-the-front:
Orison Swett Marden, founder of Success magazine, published Pushing to the Front in 1911. Its motto is that the world makes way for the determined man. Fifty-seven chapters of advice follow, from The Man and the Opportunity to The Conquest of Poverty. Marden wrote for boys and girls with no chance, country boys, and poor students.

Chapters praise choosing a vocation, concentrated energy, promptness, good manners, and doing a thing to a finish. Stories of self-made men carry most lessons. Marden's books sold in the millions and helped define American success writing. The tone is cheerful and moral, sure that character, more than luck, decides who gets to the front.
21336-the-skipper-s-wooing-and-the-brown:
W. W. Jacobs pairs a comic sea novel with a shorter tale in this volume, first published in 1897. The Skipper's Wooing opens aboard the schooner Seamew of London, loaded with cement at Northfleet for Brittlesea, her crew's faces ghostly with cement dust. Captain Wilson, master and owner, has a wooing to do.

Jacobs turns dock work, sea pies, and a mate's careful wash into comedy before the courtship even starts. The Brown Man's Servant follows in four chapters, in his darker vein. Jacobs became famous for just this mix: Thames-side humour about sailors ashore, and eerie tales where wishes and servants carry hidden costs.
21609-society-its-origin-and-development:
Henry Kalloch Rowe, who taught history and sociology at Newton Theological Institution, wrote Society in 1916. Its full title promises the origin and growth of social life. Rowe starts from a plain fact: human beings live together, and always have.

Parts treat group life, the family, and the rural community in turn. Chapters cover the making of the home, children, work, play, and schooling. Divorce and the social evil get frank chapters for the age. Later parts move to town, state, and church, tracing how each form grew from the small group outward.
21621-the-story-of-garfield-farm-boy-sol:
William G. Rutherford tells James Garfield's life in The Story of Garfield, issued at London in 1895. The Sunday School Union published the book, which reached a twenty-ninth thousand. Chapters run from the far west and its pioneers to Garfield's own boyhood.

A fire in the forest, four saplings, and a restless scholar mark the early pages. Garfield works on a canal boat, teaches, and finds friends and faith. Dark days for the Union bring him to flag and country as a soldier. Winning his spurs and filling the gap lead to the presidency, in a tale built to inspire the young.
21661-impressions-of-a-war-correspondent:
George Lynch reports war at first hand in Impressions of a War Correspondent, published in 1903. The contents open with a dance of death and the aftermath of war. Elandslaagte, a Boer War battle, gets a full chapter.

Lynch, who wrote The War of the Civilizations, views guns and gunners with a poet's eye. Later pieces wander to cities of unrest, dingy cities, and cities of dumb distances. The mix of battle sketches and travel musings marks the book. Few correspondents of his day wrote with such colour about the men who fought and the lands they crossed.
21675-the-olden-time-series-vol-4-quaint:
Henry M. Brooks gathers old notices in Quaint and Curious Advertisements, volume four of the Olden Time Series, from 1886. Brooks gleaned his matter chiefly from old newspapers of Boston and Salem. The series sold at fifty cents a volume, in small format.

A Leigh Hunt fancy fronts the book: a Roman newspaper dug up at Herculaneum. Wanted, a gladiator, or a new poem by Horace, would thrill us in that sheet, Hunt jokes. Brooks's real finds are colonial and early American, from lost horses to runaway apprentices. The volumes mix amusement with raw material for history, quaintly combined.
21978-an-analysis-of-the-lever-escapemen:
Watchmakers get a fine lecture in H. R. Playtner's An Analysis of the Lever Escapement, delivered before the Canadian Watchmakers' and Retail Jewelers' Association and printed at Chicago in 1910. Thomas Mudge, first to apply the detached lever escapement to watches, fronts the book. Playtner begins with the millimeter itself, since that word alone confuses many readers. A side shake of one hundredth of a millimeter, times two and a quarter, gives a spring's thickness: a third of a human hair.

From such fine measures he builds the escapement's geometry step by step. The lecture assumes skilled readers with watches in their hands. It preserves the craft knowledge of the bench at the height of the pocket watch age, exact and proud.
21988-breaking-point:
A perfect ship meets imperfect men in James E. Gunn's Breaking Point, a story from Space Science Fiction, March 1953. The Ambassador is a flawless machine, automatic and self-adjusting, built never to fail while a universe surrounds it. Her crew is another matter. The ship was proof against any test, the blurb warns, but the men inside could be strained and warped, horribly.

Aliens send the advance unit out in her to scout a new planet, drawn by a beeping box dropped earlier. The aliens know what the men cannot believe: minds have a breaking point. Gunn builds his tale as a pressure chamber of first contact. A spaceman studies a chess board on the frontispiece while the trap closes. It is lean, hard early work from a later master.
22017-a-key-to-the-knowledge-of-church-h: A Key to the Knowledge of Church History (Ancient) is a compact study handbook from the age of Victorian religious textbooks. It breaks the history of the early Church into short sections, each with side notes and an index for quick review. The plan suits students who must master names, dates, councils, and persecutions in order.
22130-the-idler-magazine-volume-iii-apri:
The Idler was a London illustrated monthly magazine of stories, humour, and articles. Volume III, for April 1893, shows its usual mix. Fiction leads: one story rides through thick mud toward the Shaw Farm. Outside the farm all is glutinous disorder; inside, the Royal domains show dainty neatness, a contrast the tale enjoys.

Around the stories sit essays, verse, interviews, and drawings by the day's artists. The Idler aimed at the railway carriage and the club armchair. Jerome K. Jerome stood behind the magazine, and its tone is his: easy, funny, and shrewd. A single volume preserves the light reading of London in the spring of 1893.
22162-children-of-the-old-testament:
Children of the Old Testament, issued by Thomas Nelson and Sons in 1908, retells Bible stories for the young. Its chapters follow children and youths of the Hebrew scriptures. Joseph the dreamer, sold by his brothers, opens the book; Benjamin follows. Then come the child Moses, Ruth the gleaner, and the boy Samuel, called by God in the night.

David the shepherd youth, Elijah and the widow's son, and a little Jewish maid complete the set. Each story keeps close to the Bible text while speaking plainly to children. Coloured plates, starting with Joseph sold by his brethren, carry the drama. Such volumes were Sunday school prizes in Edwardian Britain.
22433-breaking-away-or-the-fortunes-of-a:
Breaking Away, or the Fortunes of a Student, tells a school story with a twist. Its writer taught for years before writing it. He warns readers not to expect sympathy for this book's schoolmaster.

Young friends, he says, have known and despised such a creature. Many schoolmasters of fiction earned that dislike honestly in real schools. The warning promises a master worth rooting against on the page. Against him stands the student whose fortunes fill the title. Breaking away suggests escape from control, school, or home. Readers get a period school tale with sides clearly drawn. It preserves the old classroom's fears and rebellions in fiction form.
22459-the-books-of-the-new-testament:
The Books of the New Testament introduces each book of the Christian scriptures. Its contents run from the Gospels through the letters in order. The Epistle to the Philippians appears among the later chapters.

One chapter joins the Epistle to the Hebrews with James. The first and second epistles of Peter follow in sequence. The general epistle of Jude closes the survey's list. Such guides helped lay readers place each book in context. Who wrote it, when, and why were standard questions. Readers get a compact handbook to the New Testament's makeup. It serves as a map before closer Bible study begins.
22466-the-ultimate-experiment:
Thornton DeKy wrote The Ultimate Experiment, a science fiction tale of a silent city. The Masters who ruled it have gone from their great city. Their servant people still keep it in perfect shape for them.

Kiron knows the Masters had been kind to his people. As his folk go about their eternal tasks, they miss them. The city runs on, perfect and unneeded, under their care. That eerie setup gives the story its quiet dread. A final experiment, by the title, hangs over the empty order. Readers get a short tale of loyalty outliving its purpose. It asks what servants do when masters never return.
22527-beyond-the-vanishing-point:
Beyond the Vanishing Point is a science fiction story of shrinking exploration. It begins shortly after noon on December 31, 1970. Weird and startling events then took the narrator into an atom.

George Randolph was assistant chemist for the Ajax International Dye Company. Its main offices stood in New York City at the time. That afternoon placed Randolph inside a tiny world of gold. He went beyond the range of the highest-powered electric microscope. A whole world inside an atom of gold awaits him there. Readers get a classic miniature-world adventure in science fiction. Ordinary chemistry opens doors stranger than any explorer's map of Earth.
22639-notes-and-queries-number-68-februa:
Notes and Queries, number 68, dated February 15, 1851, continues the British journal where readers traded questions on old books, words, and customs. The catalog record names no editor. Each weekly number stitched together dozens of short items from correspondents who signed with initials or pen names.

In the sample, a contributor offers to fill a gap in his printed extracts he printed from the Stationers' Company registers, pointing to a register entry dated February 1587. Such register notes, dull at a glance, help date plays and trace lost books, which is why Shakespeare scholars prized the journal. Number 68 shows the machine at work: one reader's shelf supplies another reader's missing fact. The habit of shared inquiry is the journal's real subject.
22883-doctor-luttrell-s-first-patient:
Rosa Nouchette Carey opens Doctor Luttrell's First Patient, her 1896 novel, with an old saying. The old saying claims love flees once poverty enters a home. Carey grants the saying some truth, then shows its limit in the corner house at Galvaston Terrace, where Marcus Luttrell and his wife bear care with patience.

Lines of worry mark the young doctor's face, and his wife's black gown shines a little at the seams. Yet peace and a great, enduring affection hold the home together. From that household the novel builds its story of a medical man's start in life. Carey specialized in domestic fiction with a moral spine. This volume shows her warmth at full strength.
23027-notes-and-queries-number-69-februa:
A reader shares a find in Notes and Queries, number 69, dated February 22, 1851. Finding that his copy of The Rolliad contains fuller information about its authors than has yet appeared in the periodical, he forwards a transcript of the manuscript notes. Most are certified, he says, by the initial of Dr. Lawrence, from whose copy they were taken.

Anonymous satire needed detectives, and this journal supplied them weekly. Questions and answers on books, customs, and word origins fill the number in the same spirit. The Rolliad note shows the method at work, evidence offered, sources named, credit assigned. For genealogists and book historians, these dusty exchanges still pay out. The issue is a small, busy room in the great house of Victorian scholarship.
23116-ruth-fielding-down-east-or-the-her:
Alice B. Emerson brings weather to Ruth Fielding Down East, published in 1920. Beyond the calm Lumano, widening near the Red Mill into something like a lake, storm clouds shoulder up over the wooded hills. Slate-dark and rimmed with pale light, they end the peaceful summer afternoon.

Ruth Fielding, the Stratemeyer series heroine, takes her friends down east to Maine in this volume, where a hermit at Beach Plum Point holds the local mystery. Storms of weather and temper alternate in the series' reliable rhythm. Emerson was a house name for several hands, and the machine runs smoothly here. Girls of 1920 got scenery, friendship, and a hermit to befriend, all in one summer.
23147-untechnological-employment:
E. M. Clinton Jr. fights by teletype in Untechnological Employment. The messages fly between the White House and officers at a spaceport. Washington wires, in confidence, that side political factors make a fresh look at the Washwater recommendation desirable. Colonel Neuman wires back, in confidence, asking what politics could possibly touch the matter. High unemployment among Native Americans in the Washwater constituency, comes the reply.

New rockets meet old politics in Clinton's story, and the politics is winning. Jobs schemes, a spaceport chief named Dewar, and one hanging decision trade short, sharp wires. The TWX format gives the tale its snap, politics reduced to wire copy. It remains a sharp little satire of how decisions actually travel, in any century.
a-fair-penitent: Wilkie Collins's story about a beautiful penitent and the man who loves her. Melodramatic and moving in his best manner, it shows the sensation-master's touch in short form. A fine example of Collins's shorter fiction.
a-first-year-in-canterbury-settlement: Samuel Butler’s keen account of his colonial year in New Zealand. Sheep, settlers, and sharp wit fill every page. The future author of Erewhon observes all. Funny and observant throughout, colonial New Zealand, sharp and funny.
a-lover-s-complaint: A narrative poem published with Shakespeare's sonnets in 1609: a young woman tells of her seduction and betrayal by a charming, false young man. In 47 stanzas of dense, beautiful verse, she confesses she would fall for him again. Authorship is debated, but the poetry's anguish is pure Shakespearean.
army-life-in-a-black-regiment: Thomas Wentworth Higginson commanded the first Black regiment in the Civil War, and this memoir is his tribute to his soldiers. With deep respect he describes their courage, humor, and longing for freedom. A landmark of African American history and one of the finest Civil War memoirs ever written.
arthour-and-merlin-kolbing-1890-fragment:
Arthour and Merlin is a Middle English romance kept in the Auchinleck manuscript, a famous book made in London around 1330. E. Kölbing edited the text in 1890. The romance survives incomplete, and this edition says so plainly on its face.

The tale tells how Arthur came to the throne as a boy and how Merlin guided him. Wizards, battles, and court intrigue fill its pages. Then the text breaks off, and the rest is lost for good. Even as a fragment, it shows how England first pictured its greatest king and the wise man at his side.
astoria-or-anecdotes-of-an-enterprise-be: Washington Irving's 1836 history of John Jacob Astor's fur-trading empire at the mouth of the Columbia. Drawing on firsthand accounts, Irving tells of the overland expedition, the hardships, and the founding of Astoria. The classic narrative of America's first great western enterprise.
bardelys-the-magnificent: Bardelys the Magnificent, Rafael Sabatini's swashbuckling romance. The gallant's wager unfolds. This book preserves that adventure. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
bruin-the-grand-bear-hunt: Bruin, the grand bear hunt, by Mayne Reid. The bear hunt. This book preserves that adventure. Later readers can locate it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Writers of history may cite it later.
castle-rackrent: Maria Edgeworth's 1800 classic, the first historical novel in English: the rise and fall of an Irish estate as told by its loyal, unreliable steward Thady. Ironic, funny, and tragic, it invented the unreliable narrator. A landmark of Irish literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abandonment: This 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia article on abandonment — the spiritual act of surrendering oneself to God's will — explains its place in the devout life. John Wynne treats a classic theme of ascetical theology. A thoughtful reference for students of spirituality. The quiet way of trust, set forth with old-school clarity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mell: This piece covers Mellifont, Ireland's first Cistercian house. Its lavabo charmed all who saw it. Edmond Obrecht gives its history. The white monks come to Erin. Its monks taught the Irish the new Gothic building ways. Its gatehouse still greets the Drogheda road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acanthus-plan: This 1913 reference article on the acanthus — the plant that crowned Corinthian capitals. Thomas Poole traces its art and nature. Callimachus saw beauty in its leaves. A weed that taught architects. Its leaves still curl on bank and courthouse. Gardeners still grow it for its bold leaves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accident: This 1913 reference piece on accident in philosophy — what clings to substance without being it. Francis Siegfried explains the scholastic doctrine. Color, size, and place are accidents. The Eucharist gives the doctrine its weight. Aquinas built his Eucharist teaching on the distinction. The schools never let it go.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achille-desur: A 1913 entry on Achille Desurmont — the French Redemptorist preacher and writer. John Magnier sketches his zealous life. His missions stirred the faithful. A popular voice of nineteenth-century France. His retreats drew crowds of clergy. Rome made him a consultor of the Index.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-admont: This 1913 reference article on Admont — the Austrian abbey of the famous library. Henry Brock praises its book hall. Baroque gold frames its seventy thousand volumes. The world's most beautiful monastery library. Monks still pray beneath its frescoes. Its manuscripts survived fire and war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advent: This 1913 reference article on Advent — the season of waiting for Christ's coming. Francis Mershman traces its history and rites. Four Sundays prepare the joyful feast. Purple vestments mark the longing. The Church's yearly December watch. The great O antiphons crown its final week.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-august: This 1913 reference piece on Albert de Lapparent — the French Catholic geologist. Louis Delamarre praises his science and faith. His textbooks taught generations. He found no war between rocks and creed. A savant of the Institut. His maps charted the French soil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alfred-von-re: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Alfred von Reumont — the German historian of Italy and Rome. Patricius Schlager honors his diplomatic pen. His histories lit the papal past. The Prussian envoy loved the Eternal City. A scholar between two nations. His Rome volumes are still consulted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-cha: This 1913 reference article on Ambrosian chant — Milan's own sacred song. Joseph Otten traces its venerable use. Older than Gregory's chant, some say. The Duomo still sings its tones. The West's other great chant. Its melodies differ from the Roman use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ark-of-the-co: This 1913 reference article on the Ark of the Covenant — the golden chest of the law. Charles Souvay unfolds its sacred story. The cherubim guarded the tablets. It vanished with the Temple's fall. Israel's holiest treasure. Its loss is Scripture's great mystery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptismal-fon: A 1913 entry on the baptismal font — the stone vessel of the new birth. John Bertram Peterson describes its sacred form. The infants are dipped in its waters. The Easter water fills its bowl. The womb of the Church's children. Its cover is often richly carved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benediction-o: This 1913 reference piece on Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament — the evening's solemn blessing. Herbert Thurston traces its devout rite. The monstrance is raised in blessing. The faithful kneel in adoration. The Church's sweetest service. Its Tantum Ergo swells the nave.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-alexa: A 1913 entry on Blessed Alexander Briant — the young Jesuit martyr of Tyburn. Eugene Saxton honors his brief priesthood. Tortured in the Tower, he would not betray. The Society claims its youthful martyr. Oxford's scholar, Tyburn's victim. His Oxford college was Balliol's own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesar-clemen: A 1913 entry on Caesar Clement — an English churchman of note. Edwin Burton records his career. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the penal Church. A priest of the persecuted age. His Douai college was the exiles' home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canon-of-the-: A 1913 entry on the canon of the New Testament — the Church's list of the inspired books. George Reid unfolds its guarded growth. The twenty-seven were sifted by faith. The councils sealed the sacred list. The measure of the apostolic writings.

This 1913 reference article on the canon of the Old Testament — the Hebrew and the fuller lists. George Reid unfolds their differing bounds. The deuterocanonicals crown the Catholic Bible. The councils guarded the sacred number. The measure of the ancient Scriptures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc: This 1913 reference piece on Charles Houbigant — an Oratorian biblical scholar. Charles Souvay records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Paris schools. A priest among the hebraists. His Biblia Hebraica is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lalem: This 1913 reference article on Charles Lalemant — the Jesuit superior of the Huron mission. Thomas Campbell honors his brave rule. He led the priests to the martyrs' field. The order prized its Canadian pioneer. The founder of the Huron mission. His Quebec mission was the colony's seed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lenor: A 1913 entry on Charles Lenormant — a French archaeologist of note. Fernand Mayence records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the Paris schools. A scholar of the nineteenth century. His Beaux-Arts chair was the scholars' pride.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clermont: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Clermont — the Auvergne diocese. Georges Goyau gives its storied past. Urban preached the Crusade in its square. Its black cathedral crowns the hill. A see of the volcanic mountains. Its black lava stone is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-compagnie-du-: This 1913 reference article on the Company of the Blessed Sacrament — the secret Catholic society. Georges Goyau honors its hidden charity. Its members worked in pious silence. The Jansenists feared its secret power. The cabal of the devout party. Its Bossuet was the famous member.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-: A 1913 entry on the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament — Eymard's sons. Francesca Steele honors their Eucharistic zeal. Their priests guard the exposed Host. The order's houses span the lands. The fathers of the perpetual adoration. Their Paris motherhouse is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-contingent: This 1913 reference piece on the contingent — the philosophy of the maybe. Francis Siegfried unfolds its subtle sense. The free act might have been otherwise. The schools dispute the fine points. The logic of the possible event. Its future free acts are the schoolmen's puzzle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-convent: This 1913 reference article on the convent — the religious house. George Cyprian Alston unfolds its canonical form. The enclosure guards the cloistered life. The rule orders the community's day. The home of the vowed religious. Its parlor grate is the visitors' own.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-tr: This 1913 reference article on the Council of Trent — the Counter-Reformation's soul. Johann Peter Kirsch unfolds its eighteen years. It defined the faith against the Reformers. The decrees crowned the Catholic revival. The council of the modern Church. Its catechism is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-counterpoint: This 1913 reference article on counterpoint — the art of the woven voices. Joseph Otten unfolds its classic rules. The species train the student's hand. Palestrina crowned the polyphonic age. The science of the musical lines. Its Fux Gradus is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-of-dina: A 1913 entry on David of Dinant — the pantheist philosopher. William Turner unfolds his condemned error. The schools rejected his one substance. The Lateran scourged the daring book. The heretic of the Paris schools. His Quaternulorum is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-divine-judgme: A 1913 entry on divine judgment — God's righteous sentence. John McHugh unfolds its twofold coming. The particular judgment meets the dying soul. The general assize crowns the ages. The tribunal of the just Judge. Its sheep and goats are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-doctrine-of-t: This 1913 reference piece on the doctrine of the atonement — Christ's redeeming work. William Kent unfolds its consoling truth. The God-man paid the sinners' debt. The schools sift the mystery's depths. The ransom of the fallen race. Its satisfaction theory is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-freder: A 1913 entry on Edmond Le Blant — the Christian archaeologist. René Maere honors his famous inscriptions. His pen read the catacombs' stones. The Academy prized its learned member. The epigraphist of the early Church. His 1856 Inscriptions is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-endowment: A 1913 entry on endowment — the pious foundation's gift. Andrew Meehan unfolds its canonical law. The donor binds the sacred trust. The bishop guards the hallowed funds. The law of the charitable bequest. Its pious trust is the canonists' term.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenie-de-gr: A 1913 entry on Eugénie de Gramont — a French lady of note. Janet Stuart records her pious life. The entry preserves her modest fame. Her zeal served the nineteenth century. A soul among the devout. Her 1854 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exposition-of: A 1913 entry on the exposition of the Blessed Sacrament — the Host enthroned. Herbert Thurston unfolds its modern rite. The faithful kneel in the solemn hours. The monstrance crowns the altar's light. The adoration of the Eucharistic King. Its Forty Hours is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fear-from-a-m: This 1913 reference article on fear from a moral standpoint — the trembling passion. Joseph Delany unfolds its ethical kinds. donal-grant: George MacDonald's 1883 novel about Donal Grant: the shepherd boy grown to manhood, facing the world. Earnest, mystical, and Scottish to the core, it continues his spiritual saga. For MacDonald's devoted readers. MacDonald's shepherd faces the world with faith.
due-south-or-cuba-past-and-present: Due South, or Cuba Past and Present. The Cuban survey. This book preserves that travelogue. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
egmont: Goethe's 1788 tragedy about Count Egmont, the Flemish hero executed by the Spanish. Noble, musical, and deeply moving, it became a symbol of freedom. With Beethoven's overture, it is immortal. Goethe's hero dies nobly, and the play remains a monument to freedom.
einhard-life-charlemagne-grant:
Einhard, a courtier and friend of Charlemagne, wrote his Life of the emperor around 830, soon after Charlemagne's death. A. J. Grant's 1905 translation, from his Early Lives of Charlemagne, is the text here, complete with prologue, all 33 chapters, and the emperor's will. Einhard modeled his work on Suetonius's lives of the Roman emperors.

He covers the wars that built the empire, the government of the court, and Charlemagne's private habits: his dress, his meals, his love of swimming and of books read aloud. The portrait is warm but not blind. No medieval biography is closer to its subject. The will, dividing his treasure among churches, closes the book.
govdocs-archive_org-leroy-cool-meets-the:
Alexander Baron, a British writer and debunker, wrote Leroy Cool Meets the 9/11 Truth Movement as a satirical dialogue. His fictional character Leroy Cool takes on proponents of conspiracy theories about the September 11 attacks.

The piece is staged as a debate, with Cool pressing the truthers on their claims about controlled demolition, government plots, and the rest of the movement's case. Baron writes to mock rather than to investigate, and his polemical comedy is pointed and sharp. It survives as a sample of the backlash literature that grew up against the 9/11 truth movement.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AmericansforEff:
Americans for Effective Law Enforcement was an organization that backed police and prosecutors in the court fights of the Vietnam era. This news article covers its move to argue before the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit.

The group sought to support upholding the contempt convictions arising from the Chicago Seven trial, the stormy case against antiwar protesters charged after the 1968 Democratic convention. Law-and-order groups like this one tried to weigh in on the prosecution's side of that fight. The clipping preserves a small move in the long legal war over the Chicago trials and their aftermath.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIALawrenceVint:
Vint Lawrence helped run the CIA's secret war in Laos between 1962 and 1966, one of the agency's young officers in the mountains. Then he became a political illustrator in Washington, and Connecticut Walker's profile, From the CIA to the Drawing Board, follows that unlikely second act.

Lawrence's drawings appeared in the capital's papers and journals, signed work where his agency years had been anonymous. The profile dwells on the trade: covert operations exchanged for caricature, Laos for the drawing board. It is a career-change story with few parallels, preserved from the magazine press of the capital.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CranorMillicent:
Milicent Cranor wrote a report titled Head Wound about the medical evidence in President Kennedy's killing. Rather than argue one theory, the report gathers a constellation of statements about the president's head wound. It also introduces a longer study of the medical testimony on the head injuries.

Cranor's approach is to set the statements side by side so readers can see where witnesses and doctors agree or conflict. The head wound has always been the most disputed part of the medical record. Her report serves as a guide into that dispute, organizing who said what before the deeper study begins.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StoneWClement_S: Maxine Cheshire's VIP column in the Washington Post tracked the social and political gossip of the capital. The January 1974 clippings gathered here cover Spiro Agnew's house sale, businessman W. Clement Stone, and E. Howard Hunt of Watergate fame. Read together, they show what Washington readers were told about the powerful in the months when the Nixon White House was falling apart.

govdocs-archive_org-remote-viewing-pione: Birdie Jaworski, also known as Prudence Calabrese, trained as a remote viewer under Dr. Courtney Brown. An article reports her return after the intelligence community, in her account, forced her into retirement for 22 years. Remote viewing was a real government research topic during the Cold War, however disputed its results. Her story, as told here, covers training, pressure, disappearance, and a public return decades later.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_able-archer-83-fo:
In the fall of 1983, a NATO exercise called Able Archer frightened Soviet leaders who feared it might hide a real nuclear attack. An October 2022 National Security Archive posting tells how a federal judge backed the CIA's censorship of a public document about that war scare. The fight concerned one record among many from the episode.

Judge James Boasberg sided with the agency's claim that releasing the document would expose intelligence sources or methods. The posting's title gives the Archive's view plainly: here is a public document that a judge and the CIA do not want seen. For readers, the case shows how secrecy fights actually work, one document and one ruling at a time, long after the danger itself has passed.
in-search-of-the-castaways-or-the-childr: Jules Verne's 1867 adventure: the search for Captain Grant takes his children around the world, from Patagonia to Australia. One of his longest and most exciting voyages, full of perils and wonders. Verne at his most expansive.
introduction-to-the-old-testament: John Edgar McFadyen introduces modern readers to the Old Testament — its books, its history, and its meaning. His clear, reverent scholarship guided generations of students. A trusted doorway into the Hebrew scriptures. History, poetry, and prophecy are set forth with clarity and devotion.
john-wesley-jr-the-story-of-an-experimen:
John Wesley, Jr.: The Story of an Experiment is Dan B. Brummitt's 1921 account of new church work in America. Brummitt dedicates it to Thomas Kane, a layman whose service fed a new Christian conscience about supporting the church. The book presents the educational, missionary, and benevolent work of the church. Its hero's name links him to John Wesley, founder of Methodism.

Chapters follow an institute panorama, John Wesley Jr.'s bringing up, and his campus days. Then he explores Main Street, tenements, and a cannery colony, shown in the book's pictures. Later chapters treat alien neighbors, the little brown church, and Christ and the East. A final chapter asks what this experiment teaches. The book argues for a church active in schools, missions, and town life.
johnson-woman-and-the-republic-a-survey-:
Woman and the Republic is Helen Kendrick Johnson's 1897 book against votes for women. Johnson traces the suffrage movement's course in America. She also answers, at length, the claims of its leading advocates. The book appeared in New York from D. Appleton and Company. Its contents list seven chapters, starting with an introduction.

Chapter by chapter, Johnson asks whether woman suffrage is democratic and what it would mean for the republic. She then tests it against philanthropy, the laws, the trades, and the professions. Her survey argues the anti-suffrage side of a live national debate. The book preserves, in full detail, the case made against votes for women in the 1890s.
kilo-being-the-love-story-of-eliph-hewli:
Kilo is Ellis Parker Butler's comic novel, subtitled the love story of Eliph Hewlitt, book agent. Nineteen chapters follow Eliph on his rounds in rural Iowa. His top buggy is weather-beaten, light, and open, with a seat for one. His horse Irontail, Klaus by stable talk, walks steadily but not fast.

Eliph rides the hill road toward Jefferson, remembering when he first canvassed that country. Chapters name Susan, Sammy Mills, the colonel, and Pap Briggs's hen food. One chapter explains how to win the affections, the agent's own art. Butler, who wrote Pigs Is Pigs, turns a book agent's sales route into courtship and small-town comedy. Kilo keeps his gentle, dry tone throughout.
kings-queens-and-pawns-an-american-woman:
Mary Roberts Rinehart, an American writer, reported from the front in the First World War. Her book came out in New York in 1915. Its title calls her an American woman at the front.

Chapters take her to France, to La Panne, and into the trenches at night. She describes a night raid on Dunkirk and a place called No Man's Land. She also reports a talk with the king of the Belgians. Her account gives home readers a close, personal view of the war. Her chess-like title hints at how small people move in great events. Kings and queens appear, but common soldiers fill most pages.
lancelot-of-the-laik-skeat-fragment:
Lancelot of the Laik is a Scots romance about Sir Lancelot, the most famous knight of Arthur's court. W. W. Skeat edited the surviving text in 1865. The poem stops short in the middle of its tale, so this is a fragment and is named as such.

The Scots poet follows Lancelot through his early adventures at court. Love and war pull at him in the usual Arthurian way, but the voice is northern and distinct. Then the manuscript gives out, and the story ends without an ending. What survives still shows Scotland retelling the legend in its own tongue.
life-and-remains-of-john-clare-the-north:
J. L. Cherry edited this life and remains of John Clare. Clare, the Northamptonshire peasant poet, left many papers behind him. The volume includes letters from friends, diary extracts, and prose fragments. It also prints old ballads that Clare himself collected.

Clare had wished his remains dedicated to Earl Spencer. He wrote that wish in 1825, expecting an early death. Instead he lived on in seclusion to a patriarchal age. The Spencers stayed his steadfast, generous friends throughout those years. Tennyson's line about chanting in a lonely place serves as epigraph. Illustrations by Birket Foster accompany Clare's surviving fragments.
louisa-pallant:
Louisa Pallant is a tale by Henry James, told by a man who thought he knew its heroine. He begins by warning that no one knows the last word about any heart. The scene is the terrace of the Kursaal at Homburg, on a July night. The narrator waits there for his young nephew, sent to tour Europe in his care.

Music, cigars, and garden crowds frame a startling revelation about Louisa Pallant. She is a woman he has known and valued for years. Her past, and her daughter, touch the young nephew's summer romance. James handles the matter with his usual fine touch and irony. It is a sharp small study of mothers, love, and hidden lives.
manual-of-egyptian-archaeology-and-guide:
The Manual of Egyptian Archaeology guides students and travellers among Egypt's ruins. Gaston Maspero, once director general of Egyptian museums, wrote it. Amelia B. Edwards translated this new edition, revised in 1895. Three hundred nine illustrations crowd its pages.

Maspero taught at the Collège de France and knew Egypt's sites firsthand. His preface calls the book the handbook of its science. Yet he warns that fresh finds change the field every year. Temples, tombs, statues, and hieroglyphs are explained in plain order. Travellers could carry it from museum to excavation. It trained a generation to read Egypt's stones with understanding.
marco-paul-s-voyages-and-travels-vermont:
Marco Paul's Voyages and Travels: Vermont is a children's book by Jacob Abbott, dated 1852. Its preface explains the design of Marco Paul's Adventures in the Pursuit of Knowledge. The stories aim to teach as they entertain. Geography, scenery, customs, and institutions all come before the young reader.

Marco travels under the guidance of a wise, well-informed companion. Vermont's hills, farms, and villages supply the lessons here. Abbott salts facts with small adventures and personal incidents. A salutary moral influence runs through every chapter. Such books taught American children their own country. Marco Paul was among the most loved schoolboy travelers of his age.
montesquieu-spirit-of-laws-nugent:
Baron de Montesquieu published The Spirit of Laws in 1748, after twenty years of work. Thomas Nugent's English translation followed in 1752, and the text here follows the 1914 Bell edition. The work, in 31 books, asks how laws grow out of a people's land, climate, trade, and customs.

Montesquieu sorts governments into republics, monarchies, and despotisms, each ruled by its own spring of action. His most famous claim is that liberty survives only when power is split: lawmaking, enforcing, and judging in separate hands. The American founders drank deep from the book. It remains a founding text of political science.
mrs-warren-s-daughter-a-story-of-the-wom:
Sir Harry Johnston published this novel in 1920 as a sequel to Shaw's play. He had Shaw's leave to carry the story on from 1898. Mrs. Warren's tale had been laid down by Shaw in 1897. Johnston asks what became of the family after that.

He dedicated the book to a jury of women friends. He says most backed its view of the woman's movement. Readers need not know the play to follow it, he notes. Still, he trusts Shaw's fans will come first. The novel takes up votes, work, and women's freedom. It argues its cause through the next chapter of one famed family's life.
mrs-wilson-s-cook-book-numerous-new-reci:
Mary A. Wilson ran a cooking school in Philadelphia and taught for the U.S. Navy. She had cooked for Queen Victoria, her title page says. Her cookbook came out in 1920, in a third printing. Its promise is new recipes shaped to tight times.

Wilson ties good bread to a contented home at once. A note warns that one pudding measure is a printer's error. Half a cup of nutmeg should be half a teaspoon. The book teaches plain, careful cooking on a small budget. It shows how home cooks coped when money and food ran short after the war years.
my-ten-years-imprisonment:
Silvio Pellico's prison memoir appears here in Thomas Roscoe's translation. Cassell's National Library issued this edition in 1886. An introduction traces Pellico's life from his birth in 1789. He was a frail, gentle child with a poet's instincts.

Before ten he had written a tragedy drawn from Ossian. French books and Ugo Foscolo fired his love of Italy. By 1810 he taught French at a soldiers' orphans school in Milan. Austria later held him ten years for his politics. V1 calls the book the testament that shamed an empire, a classic of dignity borne in chains.
narrative-of-the-life-of-j-d-green-a-run:
Jacob D. Green tells how he escaped slavery in Kentucky three times. His escapes came in 1839, 1846, and 1848. The book reached its eighth thousand by 1864. Henry Fielding printed it in Huddersfield, England.

Ministers who heard Green lecture praise his skill and propriety. He spoke on American slavery from his own hard witness. One host in Hopton calls his lecture able and efficient. Green had felt slavery's fearful effects himself, they note. His short life story was sold to aid the cause, a fugitive's own proof of bondage's cruelty and of his will to be free.
nasa-tm-19640017341-an-algorithm-for-the:
N. L. Bonavito of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this note in March 1964. It gives an algorithm, a step-by-step computing recipe, for satellite positions. The recipe uses Vinti's theory of how Earth's bulge perturbs an orbit. Those tugs are called zonal harmonic perturbations in the title.

Earth is not a perfect ball, so orbits drift from simple ellipses. Bonavito's method finds position and velocity for a corrected reference orbit. Catalog notes stress that the reference orbit itself is accurate. Better orbit math meant better tracking and prediction for real satellites. Such recipes were core tools for the men guiding early Earth satellites.
nasa-tm-19650011399-the-solar-flare-envi:
Dated March 12, 1965, this facsimile report surveys the solar flare environment and the hazard it poses in space. It opens with the Sun's atmosphere, then turns to flare models. Radiation in space is called probably the most hazardous natural environment beyond Earth. Galactic cosmic rays and the Van Allen belts are the other main sources.

Later sections give flare probabilities and ways to predict them. Shielding choices for crews and equipment are then considered. The report ends with conclusions drawn from the survey. For mission planners, it gathered what was known about a danger that could not be seen or felt.
nasa-tm-19660024249-an-orbiting-density-:
D. A. Wallace, K. W. Rogers, J. B. Wainwright, and R. L. Chuan wrote this May 1966 memorandum at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. Their subject is an instrument that measures air density while orbiting Earth. Even far above the ground, thin traces of air slow satellites down.

The memorandum describes a device built to measure that thin air directly from an orbiting spacecraft. Direct readings matter because drag estimates guide orbit predictions and satellite lifetimes. The authors set out the instrument itself, giving engineers a way to sample the near-vacuum instead of guessing its density from below.
nasa-tm-19670010533-the-oso-1-solar-neut:
W. N. Hess, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, and R. C. Kaifer, of the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory in Livermore, California, wrote this paper in January 1967. Submitted to the journal Solar Physics, it describes the solar neutron experiment flown on OSO 1, the first Orbiting Solar Observatory satellite.

Boron fluoride counters aboard the satellite hunted for neutrons arriving from the Sun by watching for a daily variation in count rate. No such effect appeared between March and May 1962, so the authors placed an upper limit on the solar neutron flux reaching Earth. No proton-producing flares occurred in that period, so the most obvious neutron source could not be studied. A balloon emulsion experiment that seemed to show solar neutrons, they argue, was probably misinterpreted.
nasa-tm-19670026284-a-review-of-some-exp:
Linda D. Caren and Cyril Ponnamperuma, of NASA's Ames Research Center in California, review a bold claim in this report. K. Bahadur had reported making living globules called jeewanu, a Sanskrit word meaning particles of life. If true, the work would retrace how life began.

Caren and Ponnamperuma examine Bahadur's experiments and the attempts to repeat them. Bahadur defined living units as things that grow, multiply, and stay metabolically active in an orderly way. The reviewers ask whether jeewanu truly meet those tests. They conclude that the evidence advanced does not prove jeewanu are alive.
nasa-tm-19700024902-the-combined-effect-:
Kenneth L. Lindsay of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this working paper on February 14, 1964. It studies two weak forces that act on the Apollo craft joined to its S-IVB stage in Earth orbit. The pair, in a circular orbit, had to hold a steady attitude.

One force comes from the gravity gradient, the slight pull difference across a long body. The other is air drag torque from the thin upper air. Each force alone is small, but together they can slowly turn the craft. Lindsay works out their combined effect on attitude control. Early work of this kind shaped how Apollo stages were handled in orbit.
nasa-tm-19700028190-physics-of-the-clock:
Russell D. Shelton, Nat Edmondson Jr., and Fred Wills of the Space Sciences Laboratory wrote this report on September 16, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center. It treats the physics of the clock experiment, a test of how motion and gravity shift the rate of a precise clock.

The authors give a simple treatment built on observed frequency shifts of a standard oscillator. Two effects get their own sections: the Doppler shift from motion, and the gravitational shift from place. They leave out the clutter of air disturbances and measurement errors on purpose. The discussion then weighs what the clean theory means for a real experiment flown with real clocks.
nasa-tm-19700028192-roll-diffusion-bondi:
Carl M. Wood of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory wrote this report on September 12, 1969. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It reports development work on roll diffusion bonding, a way to join metal sheets by heat and pressure until they merge into one piece.

Three very close fitting packs were built, each with a different yoke arrangement to hold it. Hot rolling then squeezed each pack down by sixty percent of its thickness. On evaluation, the test pieces showed end separation and bending near the sides. Those flaws, Wood reports, did not come from yoke shape or loose fit, but seemed built into the rolling operation itself.
nasa-tm-19700033508-a-flow-velocity-and-:
James H. Monteith wrote this thesis at the University of Virginia in August 1970. It was presented for a master's degree in electrical engineering. It describes an instrument that measures both the speed and the direction of a flowing stream, built for use inside wind tunnels.

The instrument centers on a null seeking pressure probe, steered by two interacting positioning servomechanisms. Monteith analyzes the control system with vector methods and standard servo analysis. Stability, he finds, depends on how the pressure sensing ports sit on the probe face. Laboratory and wind tunnel tests then check the probe's yaw and pitch readings, and the work ends with a new instrument judged useful for tunnel research.
nasa-tm-19720003291-apollo-15-x-ray-fluo:
Apollo 15 carried an X-ray fluorescence spectrometer in the service module's instrument bay. This preliminary report, a NASA preprint from the Goddard series, presents that experiment. In lunar orbit, the instrument mapped the Moon's surface makeup. Sunlight striking the surface makes each element glow in X-rays at its own energy. Reading that glow from orbit reveals the chemistry of the ground below.

Mapping was the main task while the craft circled the Moon. During the coast home, the team turned the instrument to X-ray astronomy instead. That double use squeezed extra science from one instrument. The results helped compare highland and mare soils across wide areas. Chemical maps later guided ideas about the Moon's crust.
nasa-tm-19720018043-preliminary-terrestr:
Mary Helen Johnston of the Marshall Space Flight Center reported these crystal growth experiments on March 13, 1970, as NASA TM X-53999. She worked in the Astronautics Laboratory there. Gravity shapes how crystals grow from a melt, stirring the liquid as it cools. Johnston mimicked changed gravity on the ground with a centrifuge. Her work prepared for later crystal growing in orbit. Better crystals promised better electronics and optics.

Tin was melted in a furnace mounted on the centrifuge arm. The furnace could pivot and settle at its balance angle for each spin rate. The crucible cooled while the arm kept turning. Single crystals grew under those steady artificial gravity levels. Johnston then examined what the crystals showed. The report runs to nineteen pages.
nasa-tm-19720023165-investigation-of-the:
A NASA report investigates the Martian environment through infrared spectroscopy from the Mariner 9 orbiter. Its author names do not appear legibly in the scan. Mariner 9 reached Mars in late 1971 during a planet-wide dust storm. Its infrared instrument read the atmosphere and surface as the dust slowly settled.

Measurements during and after the storm showed large daily temperature swings in the air up to at least thirty kilometers high. Winds inferred from the temperature fields showed a strong tidal rhythm. Spectral features in the dust pointed to a silica content of about sixty percent, implying Mars has undergone substantial chemical sorting of its rocks. Water vapor estimates came out lower than ground-based figures, and surface pressure mapping revealed relief of nearly two pressure scale heights.
nona-vincent:
Henry James wrote Nona Vincent, transcribed here from the Macmillan edition of 1893. Mrs Alsager opens the tale by asking Allan Wayworth to read something to her. They linger near the fire before he takes his leave. She makes the request with a shy sincerity that adds to her charm.

Wayworth is eight and twenty, clever for one so young, and poor for one so independent. Mrs Alsager's warm, golden drawing room in Grosvenor Place is his harbour of refuge. There he forgets loneliness and the worries of his life. Talk of his ambitions and disappointments fills such visits. James builds the tale from talk, longing, and fine shades of feeling.
notes-of-a-war-correspondent:
Richard Harding Davis gathered his Notes of a War Correspondent for Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1911, with pictures. Reports cover five wars he followed for the papers. The Cuban-Spanish war opens the contents, with the death of Rodriguez. The Greek-Turkish war brings the battle of Velestinos.

The Spanish-American war gets four pieces, from the Rough Riders at Guasimas to San Juan Hill. The South African war brings Buller's column and the relief of Ladysmith. Battles I did not see covers the Japanese-Russian war with a wink. A war correspondent's kit closes the book. Davis writes war as witness, close and fast.
ole-mammy-s-torment:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote this children's story set in Kentucky. She is best known for the Little Colonel series. The sample lists many Little Colonel books and prices. Ole Mammy's Torment stands apart from that series here. The text comes from the Kentuckiana Digital Library images.

The hosted sample preserves front matter and the series list. It gives no readable opening of the story itself. Readers can confirm the author and her other works. They cannot judge the plot from this sample alone. Johnston wrote warm tales of Southern childhood and family. Her books were widely loved by young readers then.
only-an-incident:
Grace Denio Litchfield published this, her first book, in 1883. She inscribed it lovingly to her parents in the dedication. Chapter one is named for a place called Joppa. Phebe and Gerald enter in the next two chapters. Mrs. Upjohn gives an entertainment in chapter four.

A picnic, a fire trial, and sickroom visits follow. Joppa ministers to the sick and faces a trial. Phebe says good-by near the end of the tale. The final chapter shares the book's own title. Litchfield writes a gentle story of love and duty. Small events carry deep weight for her characters.
paul-the-peddler-or-the-fortunes-of-a-yo: Horatio Alger's hero this time is Paul, a New York street peddler selling goods from a basket. Through honesty and hard work he rises from the sidewalks to respectability, outwitting the swindlers and bullies of the city. Pure Alger formula, it thrilled generations of boys with its promise that character counts more than luck.
picturesque-quebec-a-sequel-to-quebec-pa: Sir James Le Moine, Quebec's devoted historian, leads readers through the old city's gates, shrines, and battlefields. His sequel overflows with lore of the ancient capital. The perfect companion for a walk through North America's most storied town. Battlefields, old gates, and shrines pass in review, told with the love of a lifelong citizen.
poems-of-sentiment: Ella Wheeler Wilcox turns to the tender emotions in this companion to her Poems of Purpose — love, sympathy, memory, and hope. Her direct, heartfelt style speaks plainly to the feelings everyone knows. Readers who like their poetry warm and unpretentious will find these verses easy company.
poems-of-the-past-and-the-present: Thomas Hardy's 1901 Poems of the Past and the Present: the poet's second book. War poems and Wessex lyrics. Somber and beautiful. Great verse, hardy's war poems and Wessex lyrics, somber, beautiful verse, great English poetry.
politics-a-treatise-on-government: Aristotle's Politics, set down more than 2,300 years ago, is the first great book on how men are ruled. Looking at law codes, town life, and the best form of the state, the wise Greek asks what makes rule good and towns thrive. All later talk of kings, votes, and tyrants stands in its shade.
second-treatise-of-government: John Locke's Second Treatise founded modern liberal thought — life, liberty, and property; government by consent. America's founders drank deep from it. The most influential political essay ever written. Tyrants beware: his words lit the fires of two revolutions. Every schoolboy once knew its arguments by heart.
shop-management: Frederick Winslow Taylor's twin to his famous Scientific Management brings his system into the shop and office. Planning rooms, time study, and bonus pay are set forth as plain tools for bosses. Dry but world-changing, the book helped invent the modern art of getting work done.
sir-tristrem-auchinleck-fragment:
Sir Tristrem is a Middle English poem drawn from the Tristan tale of Thomas of Erceldoune. It was made around 1300 and survives only in the Auchinleck manuscript. What remains is a fragment, and it is labeled as one here.

Even broken, the poem is the earliest English telling of the fatal love of Tristan and Iseult. Its lines carry the potion, the sea crossings, and the secret meetings of the legend.
